title: S-row — サ シ ス セ ソ

points.name: サ
points.explanation: サ makes the same 'sa' sound as hiragana さ. Visually, サ has three strokes — one horizontal crossed by two descending strokes, the right one longer and curving — creating an angular, pitchfork-like character. Compare this to hiragana さ, which has more curves and loops. サ appears in サラダ (salad), サービス (service), and サッカー (soccer — from English 'soccer'). The double consonant in サッカー (sa-k-ka) is written with the small ッ, which you'll study soon.
rules: サ has three strokes — one horizontal crossed by two descending strokes.
サービス (service) is used broadly in Japan: 'good service' (サービスがいい) is a common compliment for restaurants.

points.name: シ
points.explanation: シ makes the same 'shi' sound as hiragana し — always 'shi', never 'si'. Visually, シ is one of the most confusing katakana characters for beginners because it looks extremely similar to ツ (tsu). The key difference is where the two short strokes sit and which way the long one travels: シ's two short strokes stack on the LEFT and lie nearly flat, and its long stroke sweeps UP from the bottom left. ツ's two short strokes sit side by side along the TOP and stand nearly upright, and its long stroke sweeps DOWN from the top right. This distinction is crucial and trips up many learners. シ appears in シャワー (shower — シャ is a combination), シール (sticker / seal), and シネマ (cinema).
rules: Always 'shi', never 'si' — same irregularity as hiragana し.
シ vs ツ: シ's short strokes sit on the left and lie flat, and the long stroke sweeps UP; ツ's sit on top and stand upright, and the long stroke sweeps DOWN. The most important distinction to master.
Small シャ, シュ, ショ create 'sha', 'shu', 'sho' combinations.
points.flashcardAnswer: shi — same sound as し (always 'shi', not 'si'); watch out for ツ!

points.name: ス
points.explanation: ス makes the same 'su' sound as hiragana す (unaspirated 's' + flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'). Visually, ス looks like an angular, upside-down version of a spoon or an angular checkmark with an extended bottom stroke. Some learners see ス as looking like a 'soup spoon' — a memory trick since the 'su' in 'soup' sounds similar. ス appears in スポーツ (sports), スーパー (supermarket), and スマホ (smartphone — a contraction of スマートフォン). スーパー (supermarket) is one of the most common words you'll need in daily life in Japan.
rules: Same 'su' as す — 's' + flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
ス looks like an angular spoon or a swooping stroke that curls — memory: 'ス = spoon for su'.
スーパー (supermarket) is used constantly — every Japanese neighborhood has one nearby.

examples.english: smartphone (abbrev. of スマートフォン)

points.name: セ
points.explanation: セ makes the same 'se' sound as hiragana せ. Visually, セ is one of the cleaner katakana characters: it is a long horizontal crossed near its left by a stroke that drops down and then turns right along the bottom. Some see it as a goalpost with a foot. セ appears in セーター (sweater), セット (set), and センター (center). The elongation mark ー in セーター extends the 'e' vowel — so セー is 'see' (two beats).
rules: セ is a horizontal crossed by a stroke that drops and turns right at the foot — a goalpost shape.
セット (set) and センター (center) are commonly used in both business and sports contexts.

points.name: ソ
points.explanation: ソ makes the same 'so' sound as hiragana そ. Visually, ソ is a short slanted stroke followed by a longer one sweeping down to the lower left. The crucial comparison: ソ (so) looks similar to ン (n) — both have two strokes, one short and one longer. The key is the angle and the direction of travel: ソ's strokes are steep, and the long one is drawn DOWNWARD from the top right; ン's are shallow, and its long stroke is drawn UPWARD from the bottom left. ソ appears in ソファ (sofa), ソース (sauce), and ソーセージ (sausage).
rules: ソ vs ン: This is a critical distinction. ソ is steep and its long stroke is drawn downward from the top right; ン is shallow and its long stroke is drawn upward from the bottom left.
ソファ (sofa) is commonly used — Japan has fully adopted Western-style furniture vocabulary.
points.flashcardAnswer: so — same sound as そ; watch out for ン!

chapterPractice.prompt: シ and ツ look very similar. What is シ's sound?
chapterPractice.explanation: シ makes the 'shi' sound. The key to telling シ and ツ apart: シ's short strokes lean to the RIGHT (like they're reaching toward something), while ツ's lean to the LEFT.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana matches the katakana ソ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ソ and そ both make the 'so' sound. Remember: ソ (so) looks like a swooping stroke going down-right, while ン (n) curves down-left. Getting these two right is a key milestone in katakana.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: スーパー (suupaa) means 'supermarket'. In Japan, スーパー is the everyday word for the grocery store / supermarket. ス (su) + ー (long u) + パ (pa) + ー (long a) = suupaa.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: セール (seeru) means 'sale' — a discount sale event. セ (se) + ー (long e) + ル (ru) = seeru. You'll see this word on signs in shops all over Japan during sale events.
